newsitem.title: USA: Food needs in developing world seen doubling - WBank.
newsitem.headline: Food needs in developing world seen doubling - WBank.

text.p: Food needs in developing countries could almost double in the next thirty years given modest income growth, said a senior World Bank official in remarks to be delivered Monday at the Agriculture Department's annual Agricultural Outlook Forum.

Alex McCalla, director of The World Bank's Agriculture and Natural Resources Department, said that most of the next thirty year's growth in population will occur in developing nations, and that these regions will rely more and more heavily on imported agricultural products.

To fill the expected big demand, McCalla and other experts speaking at a seminar on world food security said that growth in food production in the long term must come primarily from better yields, not from area expansion or intensification.
McCalla said economic projections generally point to sufficient global food supplies at least until 2010.

During the years 2010 to 2015, harvested acreage could increase slightly, grain demand is projected to grow more slowly, and grain trade will likely increase. Real grain prices are likely to remain constant or decline. During that time, regional food problems are expected to persist in South Asia and especially in Sub-Saharan Africa.

The longer term outlook from 2020 to 2025, according to the International Food Policy Institute (IFPRI), show real grain prices falling by 20 percent from 1990 and meat prices dropping by 10 percent. Trade expands significantly, with imports by developing countries doubling. Food problems in Sub-Saharan Africa cause imports to triple.
Per Pinstrup-Andersen, director general of IFPRI, predicted global demand for cereals to increase by 55 percent between 1990 and 2020 and demand for livestock products to jump 75 percent.
In remarks prepared for delivery, Pinstrup-Andersen said that in developing nations alone, cereal demand will increase 80 percent and livestock demand by 140 percent.

The IFPRI official said that agricultural research should place a higher priority on increasing productivity in low- income developing countries, not just the well financed, developed agricultural producing nations.

"The balance between less-favored and more-favored areas must be redressed ... Much more attention must be directed to the development of appropriate technology for the less-favored areas," said Pinstrup-Andersen.
He said accelerated research is needed to develop crops more tolerant of droughts and better suited to fragile soils.

Pinstrup-Andersen also pointed to agricultural biotechnology as one of the most promising developments in modern science, but warned that biotechnology research must not be done only in industrialized countries but has to also focus on the needs of farmers in developing nations.
He scolded the "nonpoor" who are critical of biotechnology, and said countries need to develop regulations that ensure safety, but do not cripple new development.
"We cannot afford to be philosophical or elitist about any possible solution, including agricultural biotechnology," said Pinstrup-Andersen.
